headline_result_summary: Using kernel propensity-score matching and first-differences across 564 municipalities in Oaxaca, Mexico (418 governed by legally recognized traditional indigenous participatory governance [usos y costumbres] vs. 146 governed by political parties over common support), WASH impacts diverge sharply between water and sanitation and across time horizons: (1) household water coverage shows null effects across all 8 specifications (both level changes Δ and rates of change %Δ in 1990–2000, 2000–2010, 1995–2005, and 1990–2010; all |t| <= 0.894); (2) household sewerage coverage shows strongly positive, statistically significant gains favorable to access immediately after the 1995 reform in 1995–2005 (Δ ATT = .086***, SE = .034, t = 2.55; %Δ ATT = 9.05***, SE = 2.18, t = 4.15) and for the 2000–2010 rate of change (%Δ ATT = 3.401***, SE = .871, t = 3.905), which form the basis of the paper's headline claim that usos municipalities expand sewerage faster, whereas sewerage level change in 2000–2010 (Δ ATT = .008, t = .371) and both Δ and %Δ over 1990–2000 and the full 1990–2010 period (|t| <= 1.077) are statistically null.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Outcome split (Water vs. Sewerage): The abstract/summary claims usos municipalities increase sewerage faster while omitting water; in Table 4 (PDF p. 10), Water is 0/8 statistically significant (purely null), whereas Sewerage is 3/8 positive and significant (1995–2005 Δ and %Δ, and 2000–2010 %Δ) and 5/8 null (including 2000–2010 Δ and full-period 1990–2010 Δ and %Δ). Thus a synthesis coding water alone gets 'null', coding post-reform sewerage gets 'favorable_to_access', and coding overall WASH or full-table sewerage gets 'mixed'. 2. Elsevier PDF minus-sign stripping bug: The born-digital PDF text layer drops Unicode minus signs (−) throughout tables and notes (demonstrated by Table 2 'Distance city' and 'Income (res.)', Table 4 'Illiteracy' 1990–2000 %Δ, and Table 5 'Female Council Members'/'Female mayors', all confirmed negative in prose). Crucially, the authors' prose (PDF pp. 1, 4, 9–10) explicitly confirms that all three statistically significant Sewerage ATTs (1995–2005 Δ = .086***, 1995–2005 %Δ = 9.05***, 2000–2010 %Δ = 3.401***) are POSITIVE; for unstarred non-significant cells (all |t| <= 1.077), signs cannot be verified from text alone, though all are statistically null. 3. Qualitative water-cut sanction vs. quantitative outcome: Section 3(e) (PDF p. 6) notes ethnographically that community sanctions for refusing mandatory service historically included 'disruption in the supply of water' (gradually abandoned); coders must not confuse this qualitative detail with the quantitative municipal census water-coverage outcome in Table 4. 4. Star threshold quirk: Sewerage 1995–2005 Δ has t = 2.55 (two-sided normal p ~ 0.0108) printed with '***' (defined as .01 in table note), still clearly significant at p < 0.05.
study_design: Observational quasi-experimental study combining probit propensity-score kernel matching (bootstrapped SEs, B = 1,000) with panel first-differences (Δ) and rates of change (%Δ) across Mexican census/count waves (1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010) before and after Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform recognizing usos y costumbres.
unit_and_sample_size: Municipalities in Oaxaca, Mexico. Propensity score probit estimated on n = 570 municipalities (Table 2, PDF p. 8); 6 non-usos municipalities fell outside the common support [.027, .997] and were dropped, yielding primary analytic sample N = 564 municipalities over common support (Treated = 418 usos y costumbres municipalities; Control = 146 party-governed municipalities; Table 3 PDF p. 9 and Table 4 PDF p. 10). Secondary political-participation matching in Table 5 (PDF p. 10) reports Treated = 412, Control = 228; descriptive 2009 citizen survey in Table 1 (PDF p. 6) has n = 362 to 568 respondents (no WASH outcomes).
